---
title: "Logistic regression"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

We now have all the pieces needed to model an *in* versus *for* choice. The response takes the values zero and one, so we use a Bernoulli distribution. The conditional mean is a probability, so we use the logit link to move that mean to an unrestricted scale. A regression equation then relates that scale to verb type. This combination is **logistic regression**.

The Bernoulli likelihood is the joint probability of the fixed responses viewed as a function of the coefficients, and its product form uses the model's [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) assumption. A coefficient [standard error](../statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd) is the standard deviation of its estimator's sampling distribution. Response spread is a different quantity, described by the Bernoulli variance.

The basic idea is easiest to see with the two verb types. For a manner verb, the result indicator equals zero and the linear predictor is $\beta_0$. For a result verb, the indicator equals one and the predictor is $\beta_0+\beta_1$. Thus $\beta_1$ is the result-minus-manner difference on the log odds scale. We will construct the likelihood, estimate this difference, and then translate the fitted values back to probability.

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i),
\qquad
\log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}=\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{result}_i.
$$

This model joins four earlier pieces: the [Bernoulli sampling model](why-generalized-linear-models.qmd), [odds and log odds](odds-and-log-odds.qmd), [maximum likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd), and [IRLS computation](iteratively-reweighted-least-squares.qmd). Conditional on the predictors, the row likelihood and joint likelihood are

$$
p(y_i\mid\pi_i)=\pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i},
\qquad
L(\boldsymbol\beta;\mathbf y)=\prod_i
\pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i},
$$

where $\pi_i=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{result}_i)$. Before observing the data, $Y_i$ is random. After observation, $y_i$ is the fixed zero or one that enters this likelihood.

For a general logistic regression, let $\mathbf X$ be the design matrix, let $\boldsymbol\eta=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta$, and let $\boldsymbol\pi$ contain the probabilities obtained by applying the inverse logit to each entry of $\boldsymbol\eta$. The joint log likelihood can then be written

$$
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\sum_i
\left[
y_i\eta_i-\log(1+e^{\eta_i})
\right].
$$

Differentiating once gives the score, the vector of log likelihood slopes:

$$
\mathbf U(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\mathbf X^\mathsf T(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\pi).
$$

Differentiating again gives the Hessian,

$$
\mathbf H(\boldsymbol\beta)
=-\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf W\mathbf X,
\qquad
W_{ii}=\pi_i(1-\pi_i).
$$

The score depends on $\boldsymbol\beta$ through the inverse logit, so it generally does not rearrange into a closed form coefficient estimate. Newton's method instead uses the current curvature to update all coefficients together:

$$
\boldsymbol\beta^{(t+1)}
=\boldsymbol\beta^{(t)}
+
(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf W^{(t)}\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf T
(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\pi^{(t)}).
$$

The [IRLS derivation](iteratively-reweighted-least-squares.qmd) works through this update row by row. Recall that the [matrix inverse](design-matrices.qmd#from-squared-error-to-the-coefficient-estimates) converts the score into a movement on the coefficient scale.

```{r}
#| label: load-logistic-regression
#| echo: true
st <- read.csv("data/supertelicity/supertelicity-cloze.csv")
st$verb_type <- factor(st$verb_type, levels = c("manner", "result"))
```

The intercept is the log odds for manner verbs. The result coefficient is the difference in log odds between result and manner verbs, so

$$
e^{\beta_1}
=\frac{\pi_{\mathrm{result}}/(1-\pi_{\mathrm{result}})}
        {\pi_{\mathrm{manner}}/(1-\pi_{\mathrm{manner}})}.
$$

The current model has one fitted probability for each observed verb group. A model with enough parameters to reproduce every observed group proportion is called **saturated**. In this saturated case with two groups, let $s_m/n_m$ and $s_r/n_r$ be the observed group proportions. We can obtain the fitted probability for either group directly. If a group contains $s$ *in* responses among $n$ trials, its log likelihood is

$$
\ell(\pi)
=s\log\pi+(n-s)\log(1-\pi).
$$

The derivative records how that log likelihood changes as we move $\pi$:

$$
\frac{d\ell(\pi)}{d\pi}
=\frac{s}{\pi}-\frac{n-s}{1-\pi}.
$$

At an interior maximum, this derivative equals zero. Multiplying by $\pi(1-\pi)$ and collecting terms gives

$$
s(1-\pi)-(n-s)\pi=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
s-n\pi=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\widehat\pi=\frac{s}{n}.
$$

This interior calculation assumes $0<s<n$. If every response in a group is zero or every response is one, the likelihood is maximized at the boundary, where the corresponding log odds is infinite. Both observed verb groups contain both responses, so the interior calculation applies here.

Applying this calculation to the two verb groups gives $\widehat\pi_m=s_m/n_m$ and $\widehat\pi_r=s_r/n_r$. Treatment coding thus yields

$$
\widehat\beta_0=\operatorname{logit}(s_m/n_m),
\qquad
\widehat\beta_1=\operatorname{logit}(s_r/n_r)-
\operatorname{logit}(s_m/n_m).
$$

We can now fit the model and check that its coefficients equal the two direct calculations.

```{r}
#| label: fit-logistic-regression
#| echo: true
fit <- glm(
  prep_in ~ verb_type,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = st
)
coef_table <- data.frame(
  term = names(coef(fit)),
  estimate = unname(coef(fit)),
  odds_multiplier = exp(unname(coef(fit)))
)
coef_table
```

Read the `glm()` call from left to right. `prep_in ~ verb_type` names the response and predictor. `binomial()` supplies the Bernoulli likelihood for zero--one rows, and `link = "logit"` states how the conditional probability connects to the linear predictor. `data = st` tells R where those columns live. The call thus encodes the same three GLM components that appear in the equations.

```{r}
#| label: derive-two-group-logistic-coefficients
#| echo: true
group_counts <- aggregate(prep_in ~ verb_type, st,
                          function(z) c(successes = sum(z), trials = length(z)))
manual <- with(group_counts,
  c(intercept = qlogis(prep_in[1, "successes"] / prep_in[1, "trials"]),
    result = qlogis(prep_in[2, "successes"] / prep_in[2, "trials"]) -
      qlogis(prep_in[1, "successes"] / prep_in[1, "trials"])))
coefficient_check <- rbind(manual = manual, glm = coef(fit))
X <- model.matrix(fit)
score_at_fit <- drop(crossprod(X, st$prep_in - fitted(fit)))
coefficient_check
data.frame(
  coefficient = colnames(X),
  score_at_fit = score_at_fit
)
stopifnot(
  max(abs(manual - coef(fit))) < 1e-8,
  max(abs(score_at_fit)) < 1e-6
)
```

The two direct estimates agree with `glm()`, and both fitted score components are approximately zero. Thus the software fit reaches the same maximum as the group likelihood calculation.

The fitted coefficient is `r round(coef(fit)[[2L]], 3)` and its exponential is `r round(exp(coef(fit)[[2L]]), 3)`. The exponential gives the odds ratio. A probability ratio would instead divide the two fitted probabilities.

```{r}
#| label: logistic-raw-and-fit
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
groups <- aggregate(prep_in ~ verb_type, st, mean)
groups$fitted <- predict(fit, newdata = groups, type = "response")
plot_data <- rbind(transform(groups, value = prep_in, kind = "observed"),
                   transform(groups, value = fitted, kind = "fitted"))
ggplot(plot_data, aes(verb_type, value, shape = kind)) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = .18), size = 2.2) +
  labs(x = "Verb type", y = "Probability of an in-completion", shape = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

The two fitted probabilities equal the two observed proportions because this model has one parameter for each group mean. In richer models, interpret coefficients with response scale predictions because the same log odds change produces different probability changes at different baselines.

```{r}
#| label: same-logit-coefficient-different-baselines
#| echo: true
b <- unname(coef(fit)[[2L]])
baseline <- groups$prep_in
data.frame(baseline, after = plogis(qlogis(baseline) + b),
           change = plogis(qlogis(baseline) + b) - baseline)
```

This population model leaves participant and sentence deviations outside the likelihood so that the Bernoulli score equations remain visible. The SuperTelicity analysis uses a Bayesian logistic mixed model; repeated participants and sentences make the row independent standard errors here unsuitable for confirmatory inference.

## Recap and check

1. Does $\exp(\beta_1)$ give a probability ratio? No. It gives an odds ratio.
2. Does this fit make repeated participants independent? No. The likelihood omits shared participant terms even though the same people contribute multiple rows, so its independence assumption remains a model limitation.
3. Why did the direct group calculation assume $0<s<n$? A group containing only zeros or only ones places its maximum at a probability boundary, where the corresponding log odds is infinite.

We now carry these mechanics through uncertainty and model checking in the [SuperTelicity contrast](logistic-regression-example.qmd).
